blocks.p: So I saw in my dream that he hurried forward, hoping, if he could, to find lodging there. Before he had gone far, he entered a very narrow passage about a furlong from the porter’s lodge; and looking carefully ahead as he went, he saw two lions in the way. Now, he thought, I see the danger that drove Mistrust and Timid back. (The lions were chained, but he did not see the chains.) He was afraid, and thought of going back himself, for he could see nothing ahead of him but death.

But the porter at the lodge, whose name is Watchful, saw Christian stop as if he meant to turn back, and he called out to him: “Is your strength so small? [Mark 8:34-37] Don’t be afraid of the lions, for they are chained. They are placed there to test faith where there is faith, and to expose those who have none. Keep to the middle of the path, and no harm will come to you.”

v: With Difficulty behind and Fear before,
he’s climbed the hill, but now the lions roar.
A Christian man is never long at ease:
when one fright’s gone, another comes to seize.

blocks.p: Then I saw that he went on, trembling for fear of the lions but following the porter’s directions carefully. He heard them roar, but they did him no harm. Then he clapped his hands and went on until he stood before the gate where the porter was.
“Sir,” said Christian, “what house is this? And may I stay here tonight?”
“This house was built by the Lord of the Hill,” the porter answered, “and he built it for the rest and safety of pilgrims.” The porter also asked him where he was from and where he was going.
“I’ve come from the City of Destruction, and I’m going to Mount Zion. But because the sun has set, I’d like, if I may, to stay here tonight.”
“What is your name?”
“My name is now Christian, but at first my name was Graceless. I come from the race of Japheth, whom God will persuade to live in the tents of Shem.” [Gen. 9:27]
“But how is it that you come so late? The sun has set.”

“I would have been here sooner, but, wretched man that I am, I slept in the shelter on the hillside. Even so, I would have been here much sooner, except that while I slept I lost my proof, and came to the top of the hill without it. When I felt for it and couldn’t find it, I had to go back, with a sorrowful heart, to the place where I’d slept. I found it there, and now I’ve come.”
“Well,” said the porter, “I will call one of the young women of this place. If she likes what you have to say, she will bring you in to the rest of the family, according to the rules of the house.”
So Watchful the porter rang a bell, and at the sound of it a serious and beautiful young woman named Discretion came out of the door of the house and asked why she had been called.

“This man is on a journey from the City of Destruction to Mount Zion,” the porter answered, “but being tired and caught by the dark, he asked me if he could stay here tonight. So I told him I would call for you, and that after you have talked with him you may do as you think best, according to the law of the house.”

Then she asked him where he was from and where he was going, and he told her. She asked how he had gotten onto the way, and he told her. She asked what he had seen and met with on the road, and he told her. Last of all she asked his name.
“It is Christian,” he said, “and I want to stay here tonight all the more because, from what I can see, this place was built by the Lord of the Hill for the rest and safety of pilgrims.”

She smiled, but there were tears standing in her eyes; and after a little pause she said, “I will call two or three more of the family.” She ran to the door and called out Prudence, Piety, and Charity, who, after talking with him a little more, brought him into the family. Many of the household met him at the threshold and said, “Come in, you who are blessed of the Lord. This house was built by the Lord of the Hill for the very purpose of welcoming pilgrims like you.” He bowed his head and followed them into the house.

When he had come in and sat down, they gave him something to drink, and agreed among themselves that, until supper was ready, some of them would talk with Christian, to make the best use of the time. They appointed Piety, Prudence, and Charity to talk with him, and they began like this.

“Come, good Christian,” said Piety, “since we have been so glad to receive you into our house tonight, let’s talk, if it might do us some good, about everything that has happened to you on your pilgrimage.”
“With all my heart,” said Christian, “and I’m glad you’re so inclined.”
“What first moved you to take up the life of a pilgrim?”
“I was driven out of my native country by a dreadful sound in my ears: that certain destruction was waiting for me if I stayed where I was.”
“But how did it happen that you left your country by this road?”

“It was as God would have it. When I was in the grip of that fear, I didn’t know where to go. But a man came to me, just by chance, as I stood there trembling and weeping, a man named Evangelist. He directed me to the Wicket Gate, which I would never have found otherwise, and so he set me on the road that has led me straight to this house.”
“But didn’t you come by the house of the Interpreter?”

“Yes, and I saw things there that I will remember as long as I live. Three things especially: how Christ, in spite of Satan, keeps up his work of grace in the heart; how the man had sinned himself completely out of hope of God’s mercy; and the dream of the man who thought in his sleep that the Day of Judgment had come.”
“Why, did you hear him tell his dream?”
“Yes, and a dreadful one it was. It made my heart ache as he told it; and yet I’m glad I heard it.”
“Was that all you saw at the house of the Interpreter?”

“No. He took me and showed me a stately palace, and how the people in it were dressed in gold; and how a bold man came and cut his way through the armed men standing in the door to keep him out, and how he was invited in to win eternal glory. Those things carried my heart away! I would have stayed at that good man’s house a year, except that I knew I had farther to go.”
“And what else did you see on the way?”

“See! Why, I went only a little farther, and I saw, as it seemed to me, One hanging and bleeding on the tree; and the very sight of him made my burden fall off my back. I had been groaning under a very heavy burden, and then it simply fell off me. It was a strange thing to me; I had never seen anything like it. And while I stood looking up, for I couldn’t stop looking, three Shining Ones came to me. One of them declared that my sins were forgiven. Another stripped off my rags and gave me this embroidered coat you see. And the third put the mark you see on my forehead and gave me this sealed scroll.” And with that he pulled it out from inside his coat.
“But you saw more than this, didn’t you?”

“The things I’ve told you were the best. But I did see some other things. I saw three men, Simple, Sloth, and Presumption, lying asleep a little off the road as I came, with irons on their ankles; but do you think I could wake them? I also saw Formalist and Hypocrisy come tumbling over the wall, going to Zion, so they claimed; but they were soon lost, just as I had warned them, though they wouldn’t believe me. But above all, I found it hard work to get up this hill, and just as hard to pass the lions’ mouths. Truly, if it hadn’t been for the good man, the porter who stands at the gate, I don’t know but that after all I might have turned back. But now, thank God, I’m here, and I thank you for receiving me.”
Then Prudence thought it good to ask him a few questions, and asked him to answer them.
“Don’t you sometimes think about the country you came from?”

“Yes, but with great shame and loathing. ‘Truly, if I had been thinking of that country I came out of, I would have had the chance to go back; but now I long for a better country, that is, a heavenly one.’” [Heb. 11:15-16]
“Don’t you still carry with you some of the things you were used to then?”

“Yes, but very much against my will: especially my inward, worldly thoughts, which all my countrymen and I used to delight in. Now all those things grieve me. If I could choose for myself, I would choose never to think of them again. But when I want to do what is best, what is worst is right there with me.” [Rom. 7:16-19]
“Don’t you find, sometimes, that those things seem conquered, the same things that at other times trouble you?”
“Yes, but that’s seldom. When it happens, those are golden hours to me.”
“Can you remember what it is that makes your troubles, at times, seem conquered?”

“Yes. When I think about what I saw at the cross, that does it. When I look at my embroidered coat, that does it. When I look into the scroll I carry inside my coat, that does it. And when my thoughts grow warm about where I am going, that does it.”
“And what makes you so eager to go to Mount Zion?”

“Why, there I hope to see alive the One who hung dead on the cross; and there I hope to be rid of all the things in me that trouble me to this day. There, they say, is no death; and there I will live with the kind of company I love best. [Isa. 25:8; Rev. 21:4] For, to tell you the truth, I love him, because he eased me of my burden; and I am weary of the sickness inside me. I long to be where I will never die again, with the company that cries out without ceasing, ‘Holy, holy, holy!’”
Then Charity said to Christian, “Do you have a family? Are you a married man?”
“I have a wife and four small children.”
“And why didn’t you bring them with you?”
Christian wept. “Oh, how gladly I would have! But they were all completely against my going on pilgrimage.”
“But you should have talked to them, and tried to show them the danger of staying behind.”
“I did. I told them what God had shown me about the destruction of our city. ‘But I seemed to them like someone joking,’ and they did not believe me.” [Gen. 19:14]
“And did you pray to God to bless your counsel to them?”
“Yes, and with deep feeling. You must understand that my wife and my poor children were very dear to me.”
“But did you tell them about your own sorrow and fear of destruction? For I suppose the destruction was plain enough to you.”

“Yes, over and over and over. They could see my fear in my face, in my tears, and in the way I trembled at the thought of the judgment hanging over our heads. But none of it was enough to persuade them to come with me.”
“But what did they say for themselves? Why wouldn’t they come?”
“Why, my wife was afraid of losing this world, and my children were given over to the foolish pleasures of youth. So, what with one thing and another, they left me to wander like this alone.”
“But didn’t your own empty way of living undercut everything you said to persuade them to come away with you?”

“Indeed, I can’t hold up my life as an example, for I know I have many failings. I know, too, that a man’s conduct can quickly undo whatever he labors to persuade others of for their good. Yet this I can say: I was very careful not to give them any reason, by any unseemly action, to turn against going on pilgrimage. In fact, for this very thing they used to tell me I was too strict, and that I denied myself things, for their sakes, in which they saw no harm. No, I think I can say that if anything they saw in me held them back, it was my great tenderness about sinning against God, or doing any wrong to my neighbor.”

“Indeed,” said Charity, “Cain hated his brother ‘because his own deeds were evil, and his brother’s were righteous’ [1 John 3:12]; and if your wife and children have been offended with you for this, they show that they are set against what is good, and ‘you have delivered your soul from their blood.’” [Ezek. 3:19]

Now I saw in my dream that they sat talking together like this until supper was ready. When it was ready, they sat down to eat. The table was spread “with rich food and with the finest of aged wine,” and all their talk at the table was about the Lord of the Hill: what he had done, why he had done it, and why he had built that house. From what they said, I understood that he had been a great warrior, and had fought with and killed “the one who had the power of death,” though not without great danger to himself; and that made me love him all the more. [Heb. 2:14-15]

For, as they said (and “I believe it,” said Christian), he did it at the cost of much blood. But what put the glory of grace into everything he did was that he did it out of pure love for his country. Besides, some of the household said they had been with him and spoken with him since he died on the cross, and they testified that they had heard from his own lips that he loves poor pilgrims so much that there is no love like it from the east to the west.

They also gave an example of what they meant: he had stripped himself of his glory in order to do this for the poor; and they had heard him say and declare “that he would not live on the mountain of Zion alone.” They said, moreover, that he had made many pilgrims into princes, though by birth they were born beggars, and had come up from the dunghill. [1 Sam. 2:8; Ps. 113:7]

So they talked together until late at night; and after they had committed themselves to their Lord for protection, they went to bed. They gave the Pilgrim a large upper room whose window opened toward the sunrise. The name of the room was Peace. There he slept until daybreak, and then he woke and sang:

v: Where am I now? Is this the love and care
of Jesus for the men who pilgrims are?
That he provides like this! That I’m forgiven,
and lodge already right next door to heaven!

blocks.p: So in the morning they all got up, and after some more conversation they told him he should not leave until they had shown him the treasures of that place. First they took him into the study, where they showed him records of the greatest antiquity. In these, as I remember my dream, they showed him first the lineage of the Lord of the Hill: that he was the Son of the Ancient of Days, and came from that eternal begetting. Here also were recorded more fully the deeds he had done, and the names of many hundreds he had taken into his service, and how he had placed them in dwellings that neither length of days nor decay of nature could ever bring down.

Then they read to him some of the worthy deeds that some of his servants had done: how they had “conquered kingdoms, done what was right, received what was promised, shut the mouths of lions, quenched the fury of the flames, escaped the edge of the sword; how their weakness was turned to strength, how they became mighty in battle and routed foreign armies.” [Heb. 11:33-34]

Then they read again, in another part of the records of the house, where it showed how willing their Lord was to receive into his favor anyone, anyone at all, even those who in the past had greatly insulted him and opposed what he did. Here also were histories of many other famous things, and Christian saw them all: things both ancient and modern, together with prophecies and predictions of things certain to be fulfilled, to the dread and amazement of enemies and the comfort and encouragement of pilgrims.

The next day they took him into the armory, where they showed him every kind of equipment their Lord had provided for pilgrims: sword, shield, helmet, breastplate, All-Prayer, and shoes that would not wear out. There was enough of it here to arm as many men for the service of their Lord as there are stars in the sky.

They also showed him some of the instruments with which some of his servants had done wonderful things. They showed him Moses’ staff; the hammer and tent peg with which Jael killed Sisera; the jars, trumpets, and torches with which Gideon put the armies of Midian to flight. They showed him the ox goad with which Shamgar killed six hundred men. They showed him the jawbone with which Samson did such mighty deeds. They showed him, too, the sling and stone with which David killed Goliath of Gath, and also the sword with which their Lord will kill the Man of Sin on the day he rises up to seize his prey. Besides these, they showed him many other excellent things, which delighted Christian very much. When this was done, they went to bed again.

Then I saw in my dream that the next morning he got up to go on his way, but they asked him to stay one more day. “And then,” they said, “if the day is clear, we will show you the Delectable Mountains.” These, they said, would add still more to his comfort, because they were nearer the longed-for harbor than the place where he was now. So he agreed and stayed.

When morning came, they took him up to the top of the house and told him to look south. He did, and far away in the distance he saw a most pleasant mountain country, beautiful with woods, vineyards, fruits of every kind, and flowers, with springs and fountains, very delightful to see. [Isa. 33:16-17] He asked the name of the country. They said it was Immanuel’s Land. “And it is as open to all pilgrims,” they said, “as this hill is. When you get there, you will be able to see from there to the gate of the Celestial City, as the shepherds who live there will show you.”

Now he began to think of setting out, and they were willing that he should. “But first,” they said, “let’s go into the armory again.” So they did; and when they got there, they armed him from head to foot with equipment that had been tested and proven, in case he should be attacked on the way. Dressed like this, he walked out with his friends to the gate, and there he asked the porter whether he had seen any pilgrims go by.
“Yes,” said the porter.
“Please,” said Christian, “did you know him?”
“I asked him his name, and he told me it was Faithful.”
“Oh,” said Christian, “I know him! He’s from my town, my close neighbor; he comes from the place where I was born. How far ahead do you think he is?”
“By now he is below the hill.”
“Well, good Porter,” said Christian, “the Lord be with you, and add much to all your blessings, for the kindness you have shown me.”

Then he set out; but Discretion, Piety, Charity, and Prudence insisted on going with him down to the foot of the hill. So they went on together, going back over the things they had talked about before, until they came to the way down.
“As it was hard coming up,” said Christian, “so, as far as I can see, it is dangerous going down.”

“Yes,” said Prudence, “so it is; for it is a hard thing for a man to go down into the Valley of Humiliation, as you are doing now, and not slip on the way. That is why we have come out to go with you down the hill.”
So he began to go down, very carefully; even so, he slipped once or twice.
